body.text: Do you need an International Driving Permit (IDP) in Türkiye?

Foreign visitors aged 18+ can drive in Türkiye for up to 6 months from entry using a valid national license, though rental agencies typically set a minimum age of 21 (25 for SUVs) and require 1–2 years of license tenure, per the [RAC Türkiye driving checklist](https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/travel/country/turkey/). However, an International Driving Permit (IDP) is mandatory if your license is not in the Latin alphabet—and specifically required under the 1968 Vienna Convention (or a notarized Turkish translation) for UK license holders.

Even if a rental counter hands you keys on a US, Canadian, or EU plastic photocard alone, police checkpoints and insurers can ask for an IDP after an incident. As [Vignetim's 2026 foreign license guide](https://vignetim.com/blog/driving-licence-in-turkey-for-foreigners) and [Türkiye Turing ve Otomobil Kurumu (TURİNG)](https://turing.tr/en/international-driver-permit/) clarify, the older 1949 IDP is not the accepted standard for Türkiye—carry your original home license, a 1968 IDP if applicable, and your passport at all times.
How does the HGS electronic toll system work on rental cars?

Türkiye's motorways (otoyol) and major Bosphorus crossings are 100% cashless, operating on the HGS (Hızlı Geçiş Sistemi) Fast-Pass System administered by the [General Directorate of Highways (KGM)](https://www.kgm.gov.tr/Sayfalar/KGM/SiteEng/Root/HGSeng.aspx). Reputable Turkish rental cars already carry an HGS windshield sticker linked to the agency's corporate account; you drive straight through HGS lanes at 30 km/h and pay the accumulated tolls—plus a small agency admin fee—upon return.

Before leaving the rental lot, verify that the HGS sticker is affixed behind the rearview mirror and ask whether your route crosses privately operated Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) corridors such as the Osmangazi Bridge, Northern Marmara Motorway, or Istanbul–İzmir highway, whose tariffs are published separately on [KGM's official toll rate page](https://www.kgm.gov.tr/Sayfalar/KGM/SiteEng/Root/Tolls.aspx). Under [KGM's violation rules](https://www.kgm.gov.tr/Sayfalar/KGM/SiteEng/Root/OGSeng.aspx), unpaid tolls not settled within 15 days trigger an administrative fine of 4× the base toll, which rental agencies automatically bill to your security-deposit card.
Which regions are easy to self-drive vs best left to a private driver?

Türkiye's intercity dual carriageways (D-roads) and motorways are well-paved and clearly signed, making self-driving rewarding on open coastal and archaeological loops, while dense urban cores and high mountain passes are far better handled by local drivers or [domestic flights](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/blog/domestic-flights-in-turkey).

body.text: What insurance coverage should you check before signing?

Standard Turkish rental quotes include statutory third-party liability and basic Collision Damage Waiver (CDW) with a high deductible (often €500–€1,500) that explicitly excludes tires, windshields, headlights, and undercarriage. Before signing at the desk, inspect every panel on video and check whether you need Super CDW (zero-excess) or standalone third-party excess coverage.
Verify these five contract details before driving off:

items: Credit Card Deposit: Most international and local chains require a physical credit card (not debit or prepaid) in the primary driver's name for a €300–€1,000 security hold.
Glass, Tires & Undercarriage (LCF/GTU): Essential if you plan to drive rural gravel approaches around Cappadocia or Lycian ruin access roads.

Mandatory Police Report Rule: Under Turkish insurance law, CDW is void—even with full coverage—if you fail to obtain an official accident report (kaza tespit tutanağı) or police/jandarma report (112) before moving a damaged car.
Automatic vs Manual Transmission: Manual cars still dominate Turkish fleets; reserve an automatic weeks ahead in peak season.
No Cross-Border Driving: Standard Turkish rental contracts prohibit driving into Greece, Bulgaria, or Georgia.

faq.q: Can I rent a car in Türkiye with a debit card?
faq.a: Most major airport brands (Sixt, Avis, Enterprise, Budget) require a physical credit card in the main driver's name for the security deposit. A few local agencies accept debit cards only if you purchase their highest zero-excess insurance tier.

faq.q: Are one-way car rentals (e.g., İzmir to Antalya) allowed in Türkiye?
faq.a: Yes. Major chains allow one-way drop-offs between airports like İzmir (ADB), Bodrum (BJV), Dalaman (DLM), and Antalya (AYT), usually for a one-way fee ranging from €40 to €120 depending on distance.

faq.q: What are the speed limits in Türkiye in 2026?
faq.a: Standard passenger car limits are 50 km/h in urban zones, 90 km/h on single-carriageway highways, 110 km/h on divided intercity roads, and 130–140 km/h on designated motorways (otoyol), enforced by average-speed camera corridors (EDS).

faq.q: Is fuel expensive and are gas stations easy to find?
faq.a: Gas stations (Opet, Shell, Petrol Ofisi) are plentiful, open 24/7 on main highways, and always full-service—an attendant pumps fuel for you while you pay inside or at the pump by card.

faq.q: Should I pick up my rental car at Istanbul Airport or after leaving Istanbul?
faq.a: Pick it up only when leaving Istanbul—or fly directly to İzmir, Dalaman, or Antalya and collect the car at the regional airport so you never pay for unused city parking or fight Istanbul traffic.

faq.q: What happens if I get a speeding ticket in a Turkish rental car?
faq.a: Speeding fines captured by EDS cameras are sent to the rental agency weeks later and charged to your credit card along with an administrative processing fee.
